  • Sources indicate that A second study published in JAMA, based on data from 5.2 million U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two large studies published on November 5 link declining newborn vitamin K shot rates to a sharp increase in infant bleeding cases, including potentially fatal brain hemorrhages.

A research letter, published in JAMA Pediatrics, analyzed data on approximately 11 million infants from 2017 to 2025 and found that vitamin K administration declined from 97.7% to 95%, while cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) nearly quadrupled.

Sources indicate that A second study published in JAMA, based on data from 5.2 million U.S. infants, found that refusal rates more than doubled, rising from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Infants who did not receive the shot had a 47% higher risk of bleeding and more than twice the risk of intracranial bleeding.

Additionally, upcoming data from Truveta suggest the trend is continuing: refusals of vitamin K shots increased by 57% between January and June 2026, rising from 5.2% to 8.1% of newborns.

Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting, and newborns naturally have very low levels. Without the preventive injection, infants are at risk for VKDB, which can cause sudden bleeding in the brain, gastrointestinal tract, and other organs. Late-onset VKDB can occur up to six months after birth, often without warning signs, and may be fatal.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) continue to recommend an intramuscular vitamin K injection for all newborns, ideally within 6 hours of birth.

Industry observers note that the shot is not a vaccine; it is a nutrient injection that helps prevent dangerous bleeding. A single dose reduces the risk of late-onset VKDB by approximately 98%.

Experts not involved in the studies attribute the rise in refusals partly to broader vaccine hesitancy and mixed public health messaging.

“The decision to vaccinate a newborn or allow a vitamin K injection at birth is complex, with multiple factors playing a role in the ultimate decision,” stated Graham Tse, MD, a pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

It has been revealed that some of these factors, Tse noted, include conflicting messages from federal health agencies such as the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), both overseen by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., an outspoken critic of the childhood immunization schedule.

Sources indicate that the vitamin K shot is not a vaccine, yet RFK Jr. has declined to reassure parents about its safety, despite the CDC’s current recommendation to administer it at birth.

Additionally, growing medical distrust among parents has led to refusal of routine newborn care, such as the vitamin K shot, Reuters reports.

Healthline spoke with Tse to learn more about the risks of refusing the vitamin K shot and what fresh or expectant parents should know about this routine newborn treatment.

This interview has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity and length.

Tse: The decision to vaccinate a newborn or allow a vitamin K injection at birth is complex, with multiple factors playing a role in the ultimate decision.

A contributing factor to the decline in vitamin K injection at birth, as well as in newborn hepatitis B vaccination, is the conflicting messages from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Recommendations from these entities and others are conflicting or do not align with established, research-based, and proven recommendations from organizations such as the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and the Infectious Diseases Society of America.

When there are conflicting recommendations, it creates confusion and doubt among parents about what the best or right choice is for their child.

As well, there is so much misinformation on the internet, among influencers, and on social media that it is difficult to know what information is accurate, well-researched, and proven, versus what may be just someone’s opinion or belief.

Some are mistaking the vitamin K injection at birth for a vaccination, which it is not. Ultimately, all these factors are contributing to parents declining or delaying vitamin K injections at birth.

Industry observers note that tse: Declining the newborn vitamin K injection puts the newborn at significant risk of serious and life threatening complications from vitamin K-deficient bleeding (VKDB). This was previously referred to as hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

VKDB can be as mild as bruising of the skin but can be as serious as bleeding into the brain, and newborns and infants can die from VKDB.

Declining vitamin K injection at birth is significant because of the serious and potentially life threatening consequences of deficiency of Vitamin K and not being able to clot the blood.

The vitamin K injection at birth is highly effective at preventing VKDB.

Tse: If a neonate or infant has vitamin K deficiency, the ability to clot their blood and stop bleeding is highly reduced.

All newborns are at risk of low vitamin K due to low body stores, low vitamin K content of breast milk, reduced ability of the gut to mobilize vitamin K, and poor transfer of vitamin K across the placenta.

When the blood cannot clot, bleeding from minor or minimal trauma can occur, and even bleeding without injury or trauma may occur. This can include bruises, bleeding from the mouth or gastrointestinal tract, bleeding from cuts or circumcision.

Bleeding can occur anywhere in the body, including in the brain, which can be catastrophic.

VKDB can occur from birth and through several months of life. Bleeding in the brain from VKDB, one of the most serious consequences, can occur at any time from birth to up to 6 months or so and can occur unexpectedly and suddenly. Vitamin K given at birth can prevent this risk of bleeding.

Industry observers note that tse: Vitamin K is a necessary vitamin that all humans need. Vitamin K is not a vaccination.

Newborns need vitamin K to prevent serious, significant, and often catastrophic bleeding during their first several months of life.

Vitamin K has been given to newborns in the United States for close to 70 years, is safe, is studied, and is proven to help prevent vitamin K-deficient bleeding.

I urge newly introduced parents to allow their newborns to receive the vitamin K injection at birth — it protects them, keeps them healthy, is proven safe, and is recommended.

#86859. Industry News: Nihilism Is Not What You Think

Industry News: Nihilism Is Not What You Think

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Since Friedrich Nietzsche, philosophers have grappled with the question of how to respond to nihilism.
  • It has been revealed that I define nihilism narrowly as the negative and eliminativist thesis of denying objective values.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Since Friedrich Nietzsche, philosophers have grappled with the question of how to respond to nihilism. Nihilism, often used as a derogatory term for a "life-denying," destructive, and perhaps most of all depressive philosophy, is what drove existentialists to write about the right response to a meaningless universe devoid of purpose. This is why I've published an academic article on the topic. As nihilism is commonly used as a derogatory term, even in the works of Friedrich Nietzsche, it will prove helpful for the purpose of this post to take a "value-neutral" view on nihilism and achieve conceptual clarity of the term nihilism, beyond some sort of "life-denying" philosophy.

It has been revealed that I define nihilism narrowly as the negative and eliminativist thesis of denying objective values. Moral nihilism, therefore, refers to the meta-ethical thesis that there is no objective morality, no inherent goodness or wrongness, a view that many existentialists agree with. The concern here, however, is existential nihilism, which can be defined as the denial of life being meaningful and the universe having a purpose. Whether moral and existential nihilism entail each other is beyond the scope of this post, but they at least stand in a close relation.

Industry observers note that existentialists are by definition, therefore, all existential nihilists, though not necessarily moral nihilists or atheists. As is commonly joked about existentialist thinkers, with the exception of Sartre, they do not appreciate being labelled as existentialists. Just like moral nihilism is often negatively associated and equated with immoralism, existential nihilism is often associated with destructive behaviour and suicide. These positions, however, should not be confused or seen as standing in a necessary causal relationship.

In a recent development, existential nihilism, despite its negative connotations, should therefore not be seen as a label, but rather as something that is taken as a fact or at least a widespread view in the modern world, from which existential philosophy takes off. The popularity and critical acclaim of contemporary works such as BoJack Horseman, True Detective, and Rick and Morty exploring existential nihilism make it one of the most popular philosophical views in folk philosophy.

Sources indicate that in his defence of scientism, Alex Rosenberg makes the case that many of “life’s persistent questions” can be answered by science, among them: “Is there a God? No. […] What is the purpose of the universe? There is none. What is the meaning of life? Ditto. Why am I here? Just dumb luck.” It is no coincidence that these answers closely mimic the diagnosis provided by (the atheists among) existentialist thinkers. This line of argument is common in at least the atheistic tradition of existentialism.

Recent findings suggest that but in the face of evil and chaos, it is questionable whether, even with the existence of a supposed deity, our lives are bestowed with any meaning. Theistic existentialists like Kierkegaard, Shestov, and Jaspers would deny such.

The absurd stems from the fact that though life is without meaning and the universe devoid of purpose, man still longs for meaning, significance, and purpose. For existential thinkers like Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, Heidegger, Sartre, and Camus, this conflict was central to their philosophy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

California is tightening its restrictions on Waymo’s services. The DMV modified Waymo’s permit last week to ban the driverless vehicles from highways following several examples of the vehicles trying to enter hazardous situations.

The DMV specifically cited two incidents that happened earlier this month. On November 5, three Waymos reportedly drove into a construction zone. The next day, a Waymo vehicle tried to pass California Highway Patrol vehicles that were performing a traffic break. California officials called these vehicles an “imminent hazard to public safety” as long as they continue to ignore road hazards.

Sources indicate that this isn’t the first time Waymo has had to pause its highway driving program. In May 2026, the company paused freeway operations to improve vehicle responses in construction zones after similar safety concerns arose.

In a recent development, however, it seems it’s back to the drawing board on construction zone safety. As a result, Waymo is proactively taking all of its vehicles off the freeway until it can develop a solution. The company currently operates in 15 cities, but highway driving was only available in Phoenix, Miami, Austin, Los Angeles County, and the San Francisco Bay Area.

It’s unclear how long the driverless vehicles will stay off the highway. California’s DMV restriction only applies within the state, meaning Waymo could put its vehicles back on the highway in other states before the California ban, which has no distinct end date, is lifted.

It has been revealed that state officials say they’ll need solid proof that Waymo vehicles can effectively detect and avoid highway hazards, including construction zones and police activity, before reinstating Waymo’s original license. A Waymo spokesperson told the Associated Press that the company will test highway driving with trained specialists behind the wheel to develop a fix for the safety challenges as soon as possible. The autonomous vehicles will continue to operate as usual on non-highway streets.

Tech Report: Iceland’s first wind farm comes with a water-saving bonus

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1305 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Iceland’s first utility-scale wind farm comes with a useful perk: When the wind picks up, its hydropower reservoirs can save water for later.
  • According to recent reports, vaðölduver Wind Farm plugs straight into the existing Búrfell hydropower infrastructure, sharing 220 kV transmission lines, substations, and access roads.
  • Industry observers note that landsvirkjun, Iceland’s national power organization, officially commissioned Vaðölduver on September 15, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Iceland’s first utility-scale wind farm comes with a useful perk: When the wind picks up, its hydropower reservoirs can save water for later.

According to recent reports, vaðölduver Wind Farm plugs straight into the existing Búrfell hydropower infrastructure, sharing 220 kV transmission lines, substations, and access roads. And Iceland’s windiest months coincide with the time of year when less water flows into its reservoirs.

Industry observers note that landsvirkjun, Iceland’s national power organization, officially commissioned Vaðölduver on September 15, 2026. The first 14 turbines are online; another 14 will be installed in a second phase, and the entire wind farm is expected to be operating by the end of 2027.

Once complete, Vaðölduver will have 120 megawatts (MW) of capacity. When I met with the folks at Landsvirkjun in Reykjavik last month, they told me that’s enough to power the equivalent of 90,000 Icelandic households. Vaðalda’s electricity feeds into the grid and is sold through power purchase agreements.

Vaðölduver sits on a lava-and-sand plain east of the Þjórsá River, south of Sultartangi Dam. Landsvirkjun already operates seven hydropower stations in the surrounding Þjórsá and Tungnaá region.

The wind farm was sited in this region of Iceland because the seasons line up nicely.

Industry observers note that the winds are strongest in winter, when inflows into hydropower reservoirs can be low. In summer, wind speeds tend to drop, but glacial melt increases water availability for the hydropower system.

Industry observers note that when the wind turbines are generating plenty of electricity, Landsvirkjun can ease off hydropower and leave more water in its reservoirs. When the wind drops, hydropower can pick up more of the demand.

That gives the utility more control over when it uses its stored water and helps that water go further.

German wind turbine maker Enercon manufactured Vaðölduver’s turbines. The project also includes a service and maintenance agreement with Enercon.

Landsvirkjun had a decade of experience operating pilot wind turbines before building Vaðölduver. One big thing they learned: They didn’t need tall towers to find plenty of wind.

In a recent development, there’s little vegetation or other surface obstructions across this unique, exposed landscape. That allows the turbines to capture productive winds closer to the ground than they could at a more wooded or sheltered location.

According to recent reports, “Lower” is relative, of course. The turbines still reach 150 meters (492 feet) at their highest blade tip.

The wind farm covers 17.1 square kilometers (6.6 square miles). Twenty-five turbines are rated at 4.26 MW each, and the remaining three at 4.5 MW. Landsvirkjun’s presentation puts annual generation at 440 GWh and lists a P50 net efficiency figure of 43%, which is considered strong for onshore wind.

According to recent reports, the ability to tap into existing infrastructure was a major factor in Landsvirkjun’s site selection. Where a wind farm goes affects its cost, its environmental footprint, and the people who live nearby.

Landsvirkjun also identifies active engagement with communities and other stakeholders as essential to building wind projects. At Vaðölduver, the immediate task is to finish the remaining 14 turbines while the first phase completes its trial runs.

According to recent reports, the tech giant sees wind as a potential third pillar of Iceland’s electricity supply alongside hydropower and geothermal. Vaðölduver demonstrates how those resources can work together, with wind adding generation while helping conserve stored water.

Iceland is a world leader in clean energy. It generates nearly 100% of its electricity from renewable sources, combining hydropower fueled by glacial runoff and rivers (around 70%) and geothermal energy (around 30%).

Over 90% of Icelandic households use direct geothermal hot water for space heating and hot water, while the remaining homes use renewable electricity.

But it’s got the same grid capacity challenges as every other country. Adding wind – and anything else that uses power – means paying close attention to what the grid can handle. Iceland has an isolated transmission system, so maintaining stability and ensuring sufficient capacity are increasingly notable as the country develops more projects.

It has been revealed that while in Reykjavik, I met with the Minister of the Environment, Energy and Climate, Jóhann Páll Jóhannsson, who told me that the Icelandic grid’s capacity is expected to grow from 20 TWh to 24-25 TWh within a decade. Jóhannsson also said that he is pro-data center and that investors are keen to establish more of them in the country.

When I asked Jóhannsson and his team, as well as the teams at Landsvirkjun and publicly owned ON Power, Iceland’s second-largest electricity generator and largest EV charger network, about grid expansion looks to handle that pipeline, they all said that legislative reforms were being passed to speed up energy permitting processes. There is also financing in place to grow the grid. The physical transmission network is being expanded, but the process is slow because NIMBYism is creating bottlenecks.

In learning about latest and completed Icelandic power projects during my visit, it was apparent that the companies in the power and geothermal heat sector regularly collaborate on projects – everyone brings their expertise to the table and works for the common good (yes, really).

In a recent development, but what was striking in discussions about grid expansion was that there seemed to be no plans to pitch in with the Icelandic transmission system operator (TSO), Landsnet hf. It seemed that the proposal was to let the TSO come up with the solutions on its own. At most, Jóhannsson’s team stated its legislative reform “opened the door” to possible grid innovations.

When I asked the Landsvirkjun team whether they were considering working with the TSO on distributed energy resource (DER) projects like virtual power plants and onsite battery storage for its heavy-industry clients, which make up 80% of its business, they said they hadn’t considered it.

It has been revealed that I often wonder why Quebec hasn't followed this strategy. They have huge dams with world-leading power connections, and one of the problem they are facing is a lack of water to refill those dams, due to several years of relative drought. I know it costs a lot to build wind power up north, but siting a project there would re-use their massive investment in power lines. The dams would act as gigantic batteries, because they wouldn't need to drain their reservoirs when the wind is blowing.

Recent findings suggest that iceland has earned its reputation as a clean energy leader. Bringing that same collaborative and creative approach to expanding its grid would help it keep setting an example for the rest of the world.

Just within the last week, several innovative new headphones and earbuds have been confirmed, so read on for wired, wireless, and TWS options for every taste.

In a recent development, first up is Klipsch, the Hope, Arkansas-based heritage brand celebrating its 80th anniversary. But that doesn’t mean the acoustic design team is stuck in the past. Originally teased as Atlas at CES 2026 during a behind-closed-doors preview alongside powered standmount speakers and other surprises, the upcoming Stratos Series uses an atypical (for headphones) two-way coaxial array, which aligns a mid/bass driver with a dynamic tweeter on a single axis to deliver low-distortion, high-efficiency, full-range sound.

According to recent reports, the 380g Klipsch HP-2 (above) is the closed-back option, with a 40mm bio-cellulose woofer and 10mm tweeter achieving a frequency response of 15 Hz-18 kHz (+/-5 dB), plus isolation for more critical monitoring. The 458g HP-3 (below, and the one we’re most excited to audition) is a semi-open-back design that expands the woofer to 50mm to make up for some of the low end typically traded for a more expansive soundstage, and it achieves 16 Hz-22 kHz (+/-5 dB). Both promise “warm, punchy bass and crisp, sparkly highs,” and the pre-production units I heard in January delivered a good bright/bouncy balance, with rich, fun-colored but still composed mids as I recall (though it’s been many months removed).

Sources indicate that both models have an appropriately mid-century modern aesthetic, with auburn-stained sapele wood earcups and copper accents, machined aluminum yokes and contact points, Klipsch Heritage Twitchell grille cloth, replaceable microseude earpads, and protein-leather-wrapped open-cell-foam-filled headbands. Both 4.4mm balanced and 3.5mm unbalanced cables (plus a 1/4-inch adapter) with dual-mono connectors are included.

While both the Stratos HP-2 and HP-3 can be paired with smartphones and dongles of all sorts, they’ll really open up with a more refined signal chain, like the simultaneously declared $649.99 Onkyo HA-70, featuring two premium ESS ES9039Q2M SABRE DACs feeding an amplifier with plentiful inputs and three gain settings versatile enough to drive sensitive IEMs to 600Ω flagship headphones.

Industry observers note that compared to Klipsch, Brooklyn’s Grado Labs is a relatively young’un at the spry age of 73. First (and still) known for decades of producing phono cartridges, the family-owned organization expanded into distinctive, hand-built headphones in the late ’80s (and still produces some fabulous flagships). The GW200 carries that tradition into something you can carry. The 235g GW200 takes a 44m S paper-composite diaphragm derived from the drivers in the company’s multi-thousand-dollar Signature line and puts it in an open-back wireless headphone. This helps deliver expressive bass and treble articulation within a frequency response of 16Hz – 34kHz.

Being open-back means a more spacious presentation with more instrument separation than your typical Bluetooth headphone (at the expense of isolation, of course, so don’t expect these to stand in for ANC travel headphones). Helping ensure this is Bluetooth 5.4 with support for Qualcomm aptX Lossless, aptX Adaptive, aptX HD, aptX, AAC, and SBC, plus 60+ hours of battery life. And there’s a single-sided 3.5mm audio input for passive use in case the battery does run out (or you just prefer an external DAC/amp combo).

As for comfort and tuning, the GW200 comes with the Grado Labs F Cushions but is compatible with Grado’s complete line, so you can change both the physical and sonic feel by swapping them. Another trickle-down from the Signature series is the padded leather headband, which goes nicely with the matte black finish. We’re looking forward to getting a pair to try out.

Over in eastern Texas, Noble Audio has been producing artisan IEMs since the early 2010s (and founder John Moulton was doing custom in-ear monitors for enthusiasts even before that). In recent years, the firm has been showing what’s possible when the multiple-driver mentality of IEMs (some costing many thousands of dollars) is turned to portable audio, and the Astrid is the latest example. A tribrid architecture featuring an 8.3mm dynamic driver with a PU diaphragm and an aluminum-magnesium alloy dome, a 6mm planar driver, and one balanced armature in each earpiece, the Astrid brings a wired configuration and sophistication to true wireless earbuds.

The overall tonality of the Astrid is rich, full-bodied, but not boomy … punch but not paunch. While sitting beneath the organization’s top TWS model, the 4-driver Prestige Encore, Astrid still delivers a detailed soundstage. What really brings the best out of it is the Audiodo Personal Sound feature, which uses a short tone recognition test to test each ear and saves per-channel adjustments on the earbuds to make up for any anatomically incurred frequency range deficiencies. Then Audiodo Equalizer lets you address sensitivities/preferences, overlaying further adjustments on your personalized curve (3-band on iOS, 5-band on Android). There’s also an assessment-independent 10-band EQ if that level of control is more your vibe.

In a recent development, to ensure the most cohesive playback possible, there’s multipoint Bluetooth 6.0 with high-resolution LDAC/aptX Adaptive support for compatible devices, as well as AAC and SBC. Plus active noise cancellation. Battery life is rated up to 11 hours on a single charge, with the wireless/USB-C case bringing the total carry capacity to 40 hours. All that is wrapped in IPX4 ABS enclosures featuring “divinely beautiful” glass fiber faceplates adorned with a dense lattice of silver filigree, like electro-acoustic etching … a metallic polyphony of colliding chords and intersecting transients.

#86854. Rejecting Oppression, Embracing Joy

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (879 w)

Rejecting Oppression, Embracing Joy

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (879 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.
  • What makes a literary character—or a living person you’ve just met—seem intensely human?
  • In a recent study of over 400 readers, 19 percent reported “experiential crossing” in which the language and characters of a book they were reading entered their daily lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley.

What makes a literary character—or a living person you’ve just met—seem intensely human? Besides the movements people make and the sensations they describe, their attitudes can show their humanity. In literature, characters who resist social oppression make more compelling protagonists than those who quietly occupy a society's bottom rungs. Most inspiring of all may be characters shocked by abuse because, despite poverty, sexism, and racism, they believe they deserve joyful lives.

In a recent study of over 400 readers, 19 percent reported “experiential crossing” in which the language and characters of a book they were reading entered their daily lives. “It’s as if the character has started to narrate my world,” wrote one participant (Alderson-Day et al. 2017). Getting to know literary characters can broaden readers’ understandings of human life if those characters’ experiences differ from readers' own.

Industry observers note that when characters’ experiences match those of readers, their crossover into readers’ worlds can feel life-affirming, especially if their experiences rarely appear in published fiction. At a book signing in Cambridge, a woman thanked author Junot Díaz for creating Beli, a central character in his novel The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao. “I had a life a lot like Beli’s,” the reader told him. Tears kept her from saying more (Díaz 2018).

Born in the Dominican Republic, Belicia (Beli) Cabral is sold as a child after her mother dies and her father is imprisoned for offending the dictator, Rafael Trujillo. During her nine years as a slave, her “father” burns her back with hot oil when she tries to attend school. After a distant relative rescues Beli, she grows into a tall, strikingly beautiful young woman. A relationship with Trujillo’s brother-in-law wrecks her life, however, when his henchmen force her to have an abortion and beat her nearly to death. She escapes to Latest Jersey, where she marries, but her husband abandons her and their two children. To support her son and daughter, she works several minimum-wage jobs, persisting even after she develops breast cancer. Beli is abusive and violent not just to her children but to neighbors, shoppers, and police officers. Throughout her life, she retains her sense of self-worth, refusing to believe she should be exploited because she is female, Dominican, and Black.

Recent studies affirm that the suppressed emotions caused by social inequality harm people’s physical and mental health (Kiehl 2024). The effects of racism have received more attention than those of social class, whose influence many people still deny (Kiehl 2024). Beli and readers who see their lives in hers experience disrespect caused by sexism as well. Her ability to inspire readers stems not from her suffering, however, but from her sense that she is inferior to no one and deserves a good life.

Recent findings suggest that junot Díaz’s character-narrator, Yunior, hints that Beli can’t see disaster coming because even after being enslaved and burned, she can’t imagine how badly people will treat her. “Like everybody in this damn story,” he writes, “she underestimated the depth of the shit she was in” (Díaz 2007). Beli’s refusal to accept that she is in danger shows not just her sense of self-worth but her belief (at least in her youth) in other people’s goodness. Yunior illustrates her capacity for joy, which blazes forth in her dancing. A complex character, Beli terrorizes her neighborhood and hurts her children, but her humanity is never in doubt. Her will to survive and her rejection of abuse ensure that whether or not readers see themselves in her, she will enter and inhabit their lives.

It has been revealed that like lay readers, psychologists can learn from imagining Beli because in creating characters, authors build models of minds (Alderson-Day et al. 2017; Bernini 2021). Participants in psychological experiments still come disproportionately from “WEIRD” (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) populations, especially North American and European universities (Henrich et al. 2010). Novels like Díaz’s Oscar Wao guide readers to imagine the mental world of a woman who experiences horrors but retains her self-worth and desire for joy. Until scientific studies can include more of the world’s population, literature can complement information revealed through experiments by making a wider range of human experiences imaginable. Most human of all may be the belief that no matter how other people see you, you deserve to thrive.

Alderson-Day, B., Bernini, M., & Fernyhough, C. (2017). Uncharted features and dynamics of reading: Voices, characters, and crossing of experiences. Consciousness and Cognition 49, 98-109.

Bernini, M. (2021). Becket and the Cognitive Method: Mind, Models, and Exploratory Narratives. New York: Oxford University Press.

Sources indicate that díaz, J. (2007). The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao. New York: Penguin.

Díaz, J. (9 April 2018). The silence. The Newly introduced Yorker, 24-28.

Henrich, J., Heine, S. J., & Norenzayan, A. (2010). The weirdest people in the world? Behavioral and Brain Sciences 33 (2-3), 61-83.

This guide covers a range of options, from protective apparel and useful electronics to compact accessories and garage staples. Whether you’re shopping for a longtime rider or someone still getting used to life on two wheels, you’ll find ideas for different styles, needs, and budgets.

Kriega is the leading brand in motorcycle baggage, and its backpacks are no different. Waterproof inside and with 20 liters of storage space, the R20 backpack is perfect for commuting and features Kreiga's harness-style fasteners. An innovative technology pioneered specifically for motorcycles, the chest clip and straps allow the bag's weight to be pushed forward, making sure that the weight stays centered on the back without disturbing your riding balance.

It's the perfect motorcycling backpack as far as we're concerned.

Give a motorcyclist a gift that makes every ride easier to relive—and can help document the unexpected. The Insta360 X5 Motorcycle Bundle captures 8K 360-degree video, letting riders choose angles later instead of fiddling with framing on the road. FlowState stabilization smooths bumpy footage, while the heavy-duty clamp and invisible selfie stick are ready for bike-mounted shots. It’s a fun way to share adventures and a useful record if a ride takes an unwelcome turn.

This extremely compact starter box is 33% thinner, 27% smaller, and 34% lighter than most portable jump-packs, so it slips right into your pocket. Rated at 1500 amps, it can even jump-start cars, motorcycles, trucks, ATVs, boats, RVs, vans, and SUVs. Best of all, it's equipped with a flashlight and two fast-charging USB ports, both A and C, so it can easily charge your favorite USB devices while it's in your pocket. No motorcyclist should flip up the kickstand without one.

This helmet wall mount is perfect for those who want to save space. It easily mounts on any wall and swivels to display helmets or other items as desired. When not in use, it can be pushed against the wall to take up less space. A bottom hook lets you hang your jacket, keeping all your riding gear together.

Hand signals from your riding buddy can only go so far, especially when a waving arm could mean anything. Communication systems go a long way toward enjoying group rides and Cardo's PackTalk PRO is the perfect communication system for individual and group use. The waterproof model includes a mesh network Bluetooth connection for phone calls, directions, and music while also allowing for rider-to-rider communications. JBL speakers are included in the package and make communications and music crystal clear. Best of all, you can set up voice commands and speed dial to make sure those eyes stay on the road.

In a recent development, few gifts can improve a rider's safety as dramatically as the Brake Free Helmet Light. This clever wireless device mounts to the back of nearly any helmet and uses built-in sensors to detect braking, downshifting, and engine braking, illuminating bright LEDs at eye level for drivers behind you. With no wiring, no apps, and a weatherproof design, it's an easy upgrade that boosts visibility day or night. For riders who value safety without sacrificing simplicity, this is one of the smartest gifts on the road.

For the rider who owns the gloves, jacket, and boots, give them something that matters most when a ride goes wrong: Alpinestars’ Tech-Air 5 Plasma airbag system. This lightweight, breathable vest slips beneath a motorcycle jacket and deploys to protect the chest, ribs, back, and shoulders. In a recent development, you don't need to be a biker to love this Lego set. It includes a two-speed gearbox and front and rear suspension for realistic movement. It can withstand all kinds of weather, extreme temperatures, and vibrations. They'll get adventurous routes with turn-by-turn directions and topographic or satellite imagery for off-road guidance. Plus, they can manage and review routes, tracks, and waypoints on their smartphone and computer—no subscription needed.

Kryptonite makes it simple with the Keeper Disc Lock, blending hardened materials with affordable pricing. A good balaclava is one of those pieces of riding gear you don't appreciate until you ride without one. Useful gifts include riding gear, luggage, maintenance tools, navigation devices, communication systems, and small comforts such as insulated drinkware. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, old solar panels have silver and copper worth recovering. A new US recycling company called Jupiter plans to send metals recovered from retired solar panels and data center hardware to Korea Zinc’s refineries, including a $7.4 billion plant planned for Clarksville, Tennessee.

In a recent development, jupiter joins US solar panel recycler Solarcycle and PedalPoint Recycling, Korea Zinc’s US recycling and metals business, into a single, fully integrated company. Jupiter indicates it’s launching with eight certified US facilities, nearly 1 million square feet of processing space, and about 250 employees. It’s also taking on customers from both businesses, including Microsoft, Prologis, and Brookfield.

For a solar farm or data center operator, that means a single company can take equipment out of service, resell parts with remaining useful life, and recycle the rest. Customers can track where the materials go and bring them back into their own supply chains.

Korea Zinc will hold a majority stake. Solarcycle’s Suvi Sharma will lead Jupiter as CEO, and PedalPoint’s Kevin Hahm will be CFO. Microsoft and Prologis Ventures are among Solarcycle’s existing investors.

In a recent development, as Electrek reported in January, Solarcycle’s Cedartown, Georgia, plant was processing thousands of old solar panels a week when it opened. Solarcycle said the plant could handle up to 5 gigawatts’ worth of panels annually at full capacity, recovering materials such as glass, aluminum, copper, and silver.

Sources indicate that the Tennessee plant adds a US refining step. Korea Zinc is developing the facility, called Project Crucible, with US government backing. It expects to start production in phases in 2029. The plant is designed to process about 1.1 million tons of raw materials per year and produce roughly 540,000 tons of finished products.

Interested in the Ford Fathom but want some of that famed Toyota reliability? You, my friend, might be moving to Brazil in the near future. Toyota just confirmed the eventual arrival of the Corolla Deck, a hybrid urban pickup based on the Corolla Cross.

Not much is known about the Corolla Deck yet, but we like what we’ve seen so far. The announcement (covered by Motor1 Brazil) came during the inauguration of Toyota’s latest Sorocaba, São Paulo, manufacturing facility. Toyota debuted a version of the truck wearing XRX badging (the top Corolla Cross trim sold in Latin America), as well as HEV badging, suggesting the same hybrid setup as the Corolla and Corolla Cross.

See all results for newly introduced 2027 Toyota Corolla Cross for sale near 19103.

In that market, the hybrid Corolla Sedan and Corolla Cross subcompact SUV come with a naturally aspirated 1.8-liter combustion engine paired to an electric motor and a 1.3-kWh battery. In both vehicles, the system combines for a modest 122 horsepower, which is routed through an e-CVT automatic transmission to the front wheels. Sure, that’s not a ton of power, but it’s considerably more go juice than the Scion Kei-01, the mini pickup that Toyota does have plans to bring to the United States. Since the Scion is limited to just 25 mph, the Corolla Deck should be quite a bit more practical on U.S. roads.

You won’t have to move to Brazil specifically if you want to buy the Corolla Deck; you just can’t live in the United States. The Naked Truth About Taking Your Inner Ape for a Walk

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Sources indicate that walking is a key milestone for human development, an activity done for recreation, and can be an Olympic sport.
  • A key characteristic of human gait is that we land on our heels at the end of swing—something found also in African apes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Sources indicate that walking is a key milestone for human development, an activity done for recreation, and can be an Olympic sport. Walking is a critical and integral behavior across the animal kingdom. It's also something that can be leveraged with deliberate practice. And it's been going on for millions of years since our proto-human ancestors were learning to stand upright, walk bipedally, and land on their heels.

A key characteristic of human gait is that we land on our heels at the end of swing—something found also in African apes. My research career included diving deep into the neuromechanics of human walking and especially the way sensory feedback and spinal cord motor control vary functionally while we move. I was fascinated by the fact that the most critically controlled part of the step cycle is heel strike—just when your foot lands and weight begins to shift onto the fresh stance leg.

Sources indicate that so my eye was drawn to the recent work, "Heel-strike Mechanics Reveal Evolutionary Trade-offs in Hominin Bipedalism" by Nicholas B. Holowka et al.

Sources indicate that these researchers studied bipedal and quadrupedal locomotion of chimpanzees and humans and examined forces and angles of the foot at the beginning of stance. They found that chimpanzees had much larger ranges of foot-strike angles than humans and often did not land heel-first.

Sources indicate that impact forces and loading rates are much higher with heel-striking, but metabolic cost is lower. This work suggests that the primitive leg anatomy of early hominins meant either high impact forces or poor walking economy. A convergent solution for less mechanically stressful, more economical, and larger travel ranges arrived via "evolution of larger heels and lower limb joints.".

Sources indicate that but can we turn heel-strike walking into striking with our heels? The timing of when you put your foot down at heel strike is the most dangerous part of the entire step cycle. If we make a mistake, or we slip on something, or the ground gives when we put our heel down and our body begins to shift weight onto that leg, we can have a catastrophic failure and a fall. Which is the ultimate failure for the locomotive system.

Recent findings suggest that so it's critical to avoid a catastrophe, and evolution of bipedal locomotion has incorporated neurological connections that assist in controlling this. But the opposite side of that is that it's also an opportunity. And that's where self-protection and martial arts training factor in.

That critical part of the step cycle is an excellent time to take that heel and stomp it onto an attacker's instep or the top of their foot. You can jam all your weight that's already moving forward to normally be accepted by your stance leg. But now it's to destabilize your opponent.

Industry observers note that this is something I teach when guiding martial arts practice: harnessing the natural movement of the body as the base layer for tactical reaction. Martial arts like Bagua Zhang center core practice on circle walking, where locomotion is central to the performance of discrete actions. We can connect our evolutionary advantage in walking to become a powerful application of self-protective action. This allows us to fully express the functional connectivity within the nervous system, mostly subliminal and automatic, in deliberate mindful action.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On the evening of October 11, a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) was born at the Chester Zoo in England.
  • The sex and weight have not been revealed yet, and the calf also does not have a name.
  • It has been revealed that at birth, greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the evening of October 11, a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) was born at the Chester Zoo in England. Even more exciting, CCTV cameras captured the poignant moment for this threatened species. The footage shows rhino mom Asha giving birth, and the calf’s first unsure steps into the world.

The sex and weight have not been revealed yet, and the calf also does not have a name.

It has been revealed that at birth, greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds. By comparison, the largest adult greater one-horned rhinos weigh over two tons, or as much as a car.

Recent findings suggest that the team used a combination of experience and non-invasive testing to help proposal out the pregnancy. They closely monitored Asha’s behavior and regularly collected samples of her poop. By testing hormone levels in the samples, they could track Asha’s reproductive cycle and identify when she would be most open to mating. This helped the team safely introduce her to Beni the rhino, while a separate analysis helped confirm the pregnancy.

It has been revealed that “Asha was pregnant for about 15 months, so it’s a long wait! We had our fingers crossed when she demonstrated signs of labour and we knew we were likely to welcome the calf very soon,” Emma Evison, Team Manager for rhinos mentioned in an e-mailed statement. “It was a substantial moment for us—and for the conservation breeding programme—when the calf arrived. Any birth can be risky, even for an experienced mum, but fortunately everything went smoothly. The calf was up and about within an hour and feeding shortly afterwards. Asha knows exactly what she’s doing.”.

Both mother and calf are reportedly in good health. They remained inside for the first few days following the birth to stay warm, but are now venturing to a special behind-the-scenes paddock outside of the enclosure. The calf is Asha’s fourth with father Beni. Sadly, Beni died in September following a sudden and brief illness.

Industry observers note that “Beni was a lovely rhino. He was calm and approachable, helped train animal care specialists and even took part in animal behaviour studies,” added Tom Garland, Assistant Manager of the rhino team at Chester Zoo. “It’s lovely to know that his legacy lives on through this calf.”.

While not the largest rhino species in the world, greater one-horned rhinos stand about six feet tall at the shoulder and are the biggest in Asia. They have the smallest horns of any rhino, but also have the biggest teeth. The males will sometimes use these chompers to bite each other while sparring. Presently, about 4,000 greater one-horned rhinos are alive today. They live in India and Nepal, in forests, wetlands, and grasslands. In the early 1990s, trophy hunting and habitat loss almost drove them to extinction.. Poaching for their prized horns also threatened their survival.

According to recent reports, while the IUCN Red List of Endangered Species presently lists them as Vulnerable, they remain  at risk of extinction. Many of the rhinos are concentrated into a relatively small number of protected areas, putting their genetic diversity at risk. A lack of genetic diversity can lead to inbreeding and worse health outcomes in general. This newly introduced calf is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding program to help maintain a healthy and genetically diverse population of greater one-horned rhinos living in human care.

Recent findings suggest that “Supporting Asha’s pregnancy has been really exciting,” added conservation scientist John O’Hanlan. “She’s one of relatively few greater one-horned rhinos in Europe actively breeding, so every successful birth is crucial in maintaining a healthy and genetically diverse population.”.

Mercedes-Benz Will Sell a C111 Rotary Supercar Prototype for the First Time in History

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s no shortage of rare, collectable, crazy-desirable classic Mercedes-Benz vehicles out there for the discerning car collector.
  • In a recent development, but no matter how rich, how connected, how much of a master of the universe you are, you’ve never been able to buy one of Mercedes-Benz’s most ground-breaking machines: the rotary-powered C111.
  • Fans of the brand certainly need no introduction to this wedge-shaped beauty, but for those of you who might not be as current on your Mercedes history, the C111 was revealed at the 1969 International Motor Show (IAA) in Frankfurt, less than two months after Neil Armstrong plopped his boots on the moon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s no shortage of rare, collectable, crazy-desirable classic Mercedes-Benz vehicles out there for the discerning car collector. Some of the Three-Pointed Star’s cars have gone down in history among the most expensive automobiles ever sold; there’s the $11.8 million 1936 Mercedes-Benz 540 K Special Roadster by Sindelfingen, the $10.2 million 2002 Mercedes-Benz CLK GTR Roadster, and of course, the 1955 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupé that sold for over $140 million back in 2022, making it the world’s most valuable car.

In a recent development, but no matter how rich, how connected, how much of a master of the universe you are, you’ve never been able to buy one of Mercedes-Benz’s most ground-breaking machines: the rotary-powered C111. Or at least, that was the case. Come next year, for the very first time, one lucky person will be able to take the Apollo-era wundercar home.

Fans of the brand certainly need no introduction to this wedge-shaped beauty, but for those of you who might not be as current on your Mercedes history, the C111 was revealed at the 1969 International Motor Show (IAA) in Frankfurt, less than two months after Neil Armstrong plopped his boots on the moon. The idea was to create a gullwinged successor to the iconic W198-gen 300SL that dominated racing in the 1950s, packed with then-impressive technology: Wankel rotary engines, fiberglass bodywork, and multi-link rear suspension, all wrapped in a gorgeous period design.

Yet while 17 prototypes were ultimately made, the car never entered production. Rumor has it that interested parties practically channeled Philip J. Fry shouting “Shut up and take my money” by mailing blank checks to the organization’s home office, but Mercedes stated no dice, citing the Wankel motor’s inability to play nicely with the 1973 oil crisis. (That also kept the motor from winding up in the S-Class, as Mercedes-Benz Classic head of collection Dennis Heck said.) Instead, the copies served as company test beds for years, performing tasks like high-speed testing at Nardo with a variety of different powertrains and aerodynamic kits.

The car in question that will be up for grabs is the third one ever made, a C111-II variant known internally as “Car 33” that comes equipped with its original 2.4-liter 4-rotor engine making 345 horsepower and 289 lb-ft connected to a 5-speed manual gearbox. It was used as part of the Mercedes test fleet, trialing features like anti-lock brakes and a component to empty its twin fuel tanks at even rates—a handy feature in a car capable of 186 miles per hour.

It has been revealed that the car was restored to working order two years ago at the Mercedes-Benz Classic Center, although the patina of the Weißherbst-colored exterior and gray-and-white houndstooth patterned interior was kept delightfully intact. As of last month’s photo shoot, its odometer indicated 24,766 kilometers—15,355 miles.

The C111 in question will hit the auction block on February 3, 2027, at the Palais du Louvre as part of RM Sotheby’s Retromobile Paris auctions, with the funds raised by the sale used to help the automaker further develop the Mercedes-Benz museum in Stuttgart, including the creation of a digital twin of the museum that will let people access it virtually.

Industry observers note that given its provenance, I would not expect it to go cheap. Neither does the tech giant. “We do believe it will come to a significant double-digit euro [price at auction],” CEO of Mercedes-Benz Heritage GmbH Marcus Breitschwerdt told Road & Track.

Sources indicate that “It’s gonna be in excess of twenty-five [million] euros,” RM Sotheby’s president Gord Duff added. “There will be strong activity. It’s one of those things you could never get until now.”.

And if you’re thinking, Ehh, they’ve broken the seal on sales, I’ll wait until they auction off another one—well, you’d better be prepared to hold off until 2051 or so, because Mercedes indicates this sale includes a contractual commitment that it will not sell any more C111s for the next 25 years. Should you be interested in bidding, you can find out more here.

  • We’ve known about the newly introduced content side of today’s patch for quite some time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Battlefield 6’s first season has entered its second phase. The game received a major patch earlier today, version 1.1.2.0, which delivers a host of changes to the game, many of which have been expected.

The enhancement, of course, also adds new content to the game in the form of the map Eastwood, as well as new hardware and fresh features for the multiplayer sandbox.

We’ve known about the newly introduced content side of today’s patch for quite some time. The patch kicks off the California Resistance stage of Season 1, which is the second of three. The new Eastwood map takes place in California, and it’s a map cut from the larger Battlefield Redsec battle royale map of Fort Lyndon.

There’s a new limited-time mode called Sabotage - a tactical, 8v8 mode where two teams attempt to destroy as many bomb sites as possible. The other massive new feature that arrives today is Battle Pickups.

Recent findings suggest that these are powerful weapons which can be found in specific game modes (and in Portal), scattered around the map for players to pick up and use. They have limited ammo that cannot be replenished, and deliver incredible firepower.

According to recent reports, redsec players have a upcoming Gauntlet mission to look forward to that joins the existing modes. It’s called Rodeo and it involves a lot of vehicular action. Finally, everyone gets to unlock two new weapons: the the DB-12 shotgun, and the M327 Trait revolver sidearm. There’s also a new angled grip attachment.

The fixes and tweaks side of the patch is arguably the more interesting. Controller aim assist has received a significant overhaul that essentially resets everything to open beta settings. The goal is to make infantry targeting more consistent.

Controller players actually get the bulk of the changes in this update, which also improves input latency and stick response. Several challenges that reset aim assist values, or make it behave erratically, have been addressed.

The conversation around weapon bloom/spread doesn’t look like it’s ever going to end, because Battlefield Studios is yet again tuning gunplay to fix unintended dispersion behaviour, and decrease its intensity across the board.

Certain Challenges have had their description rewritten so their requirements can be better understood. Beyond that, you can expect several deployables to behave much more consistently, including several bug fixes there, too.

Head to the official blog for the full rundown of patch 1.1.2.0.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GLP-1 owners have a upcoming symptom to watch for: Sudden vision loss in one eye.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) unveiled on November 9 that it will require drugmakers to add information to the warning labels of Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound and other GLP-1 medications about “a potential increased risk” of a rare eye condition called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).GLP-1 medications are approved to treat type 2 diabetes and to help people lose weight and keep it off.NAION joins a growing list of side effects linked to GLP-1s, adding a second eye warning to several labels.The U.S. labels for Ozempic, Rybelsus, Trulicity, Mounjaro, and Zepbound already warn about diabetic retinopathy, a diabetes-related eye disease, according to each drug’s prescribing information.The two conditions affect different parts of the eye. Diabetic retinopathy damages tiny blood vessels in the retina, the layer at the back of the eye that senses light, according to the National Eye Institute. NAION damages the optic nerve when it doesn’t get enough blood, according to the FDA’s announcement.Mihail Zilbermint, MD, director of endocrine hospitalists at Johns Hopkins, told Healthline he hasn’t seen NAION in his patients. He has seen vision worsen in some people after they start a GLP-1.“But we believe that’s probably related to rapid improvement in their sugar control, which can also be seen in someone who is starting insulin,” Zilbermint stated.

A 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology “initially triggered” the FDA’s review, the agency told Healthline.

According to recent reports, the study found a higher risk of NAION in people prescribed semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, than in people prescribed other diabetes or weight-loss drugs.The authors wrote that more research is needed to determine whether semaglutide causes NAION.Joseph F. Rizzo III, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear in Boston, served as the study’s corresponding author.

Recent findings suggest that in a 2024 podcast, Rizzo said he and a resident saw three patients with NAION who were taking semaglutide for about a week.“And because NAION is a fairly uncommon disorder in the general population, the fact that we had three within a relatively short period of time led me to suspect that there was a higher risk of developing NAION in patients on semaglutide,” Rizzo said. The FDA analyzed clinical trials for multiple GLP-1 drugs and noted that NAION cases were reported with every GLP-1 on the market, according to its announcement. Those findings led the FDA to require the warning for the entire drug class, the agency told Healthline.

About 70% to 80% of people with NAION first notice vision loss when they wake up, according to StatPearls. The FDA listed these symptoms:.

No treatment has been proven to reverse vision loss from NAION, according to StatPearls.

“Patients experiencing sudden, painless vision loss in one eye should contact their healthcare professional immediately and should not stop their medication without consulting their provider first,” the FDA told Healthline.

In the announcement, the agency told doctors to promptly refer patients with suspected NAION to an ophthalmologist.

The FDA listed these possible risk factors for NAION:.

The FDA told Healthline that many people who take GLP-1s also have these conditions, which made reports of NAION in GLP-1 users “challenging” to interpret.

Industry observers note that across 126 clinical trials, the FDA found about 6 NAION cases per 100,000 people taking a GLP-1 for a year, and about 4 per 100,000 people taking a placebo or another diabetes drug for a year.In real-world data, NAION was more common with GLP-1s than with one type of diabetes pill, but the FDA found no significant increase compared with another type, the agency told Healthline.Zilbermint mentioned patients who saw the news have worried about losing their vision. He tells them that “many of the serious harms, including the potential harm of NAION, are rare.”“The overall risk is still very small,” he said.

Regulators in other countries have added NAION warnings, mostly for semaglutide:.

The FDA told Healthline the benefits of GLP-1s “continue to outweigh their risks when used as directed.”The FDA has also approved some GLP-1s to lower the risk of heart attack and stroke, reduce the risk of worsening kidney disease, and treat sleep apnea and a type of liver disease.Zilbermint stated that “for most of my patients with obesity, diabetes and heart disease, the benefits clearly outweigh the risks.”“But we definitely have to decide patient by patient,” he added.

The labeling change applies to these medications, according to the FDA’s announcement:.

As of publication, the FDA’s online label database did not yet show the upcoming warning on the drugs’ labels.

#86843. In Defense of Clever Hans

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1389 w)

In Defense of Clever Hans

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1389 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Proponents of facilitated communication (FC)—a discredited intervention in which a nondisabled facilitator helps a profoundly autistic person spell out sophisticated messages on a letter board or keyboard—really do not like it when critics point to the famous case of Clever Hans, calling this analogy “indefensibly dehumanizing” and, as Marina Weiler recently argued on this site, “cruel.”.
  • But the Clever Hans argument is not, as critics charge, about “comparing autistic people to animals.” It is about illustrating how subtly and unintentionally behavior can be cued.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Proponents of facilitated communication (FC)—a discredited intervention in which a nondisabled facilitator helps a profoundly autistic person spell out sophisticated messages on a letter board or keyboard—really do not like it when critics point to the famous case of Clever Hans, calling this analogy “indefensibly dehumanizing” and, as Marina Weiler recently argued on this site, “cruel.”.

But the Clever Hans argument is not, as critics charge, about “comparing autistic people to animals.” It is about illustrating how subtly and unintentionally behavior can be cued.

Industry observers note that no one explicitly taught this horse to stop tapping his hoof at some predetermined signal. He learned from observing tiny, unconscious movements of his trainer’s head that a commission of experts sent to observe Hans’ seemingly extraordinary abilities couldn’t spot, even under close scrutiny (a graduate student in psychology finally figured it out). If a horse can learn to respond to signs barely observable to the human eye, FC skeptics (such as myself) point out, humans can certainly do the same, and likely to even more imperceptible—or not so imperceptible—cues, such as changes in breathing, pitch, or posture; verbal prompts; or shifting the letter board in the air.

Importantly, facilitators are also subject to influence in the form of common psychological biases. An amazing example of how strong the desire to believe can affect facilitators aired earlier this year on "The Today Show." After publishing his first novel, speller Woody Brown and his mother, who facilitates for him, were interviewed by Jenna Bush Hager. As a camera positioned behind the pair documented, there was absolutely no correlation between Woody’s random jabs at the letter board and the articulate responses his mother “read.”.

Recent findings suggest that in short, the Clever Hans story is raised as part of the case that authorship in spelling cannot be judged based solely on how it looks to the observer. Especially because it is so easy to expose facilitator control: Just ask the speller to produce information that is definitively unknown to their facilitator, i.e., by showing them an object that the facilitator hasn’t seen and asking them to identify it. This has been done in dozens of studies dating back to the 1990s, and FC has failed every time. A recent review confirms that independent authorship in any form of FC—including more recent variants, Rapid Prompting Method (RPM) and Spelling to Communicate (S2C)—has never been demonstrated under controlled conditions.

Sources indicate that in response, the spelling community has simply refused to participate in any more of these tests. I will never understand why the debate didn’t end there. That is just not how the scientific method operates. Good research starts with the null hypothesis—the assumption that the intervention under investigation doesn’t work. Once evidence is obtained of a positive effect, conscientious researchers try to account for any other possible factor that could explain their findings, such as the placebo effect—or, in the case of FC, facilitator control. It is only once these other explanations have been ruled out that efficacy can be established. Instead, FC researchers offer “qualitative research” (i.e., interviews with spellers who use FC products to prove FC) and indirect, technology-intensive studies involving eye-tracking apparatuses, computer algorithms, FMRI, and accelerometers that claim to prove FC works even though the facilitators in these tests are never blinded.

By far, the most baffling question I’m asked by spelling proponents is, “Why do you care?” In other words: If I object to spelling, I should just not use it with my profoundly autistic son, Jonah. Why do I have to oppose it so publicly?

I’ve thought about this a lot recently, because spelling has become the wedge concern that is fracturing the profound autism community. And I am heartsick, because I know this diminishes our power to effect the changes our kids desperately need to flourish.

Sources indicate that but spelling is not like vitamins, diet, brushing, or any of the countless alternative therapies that parents of profoundly autistic children, myself included, have experimented with since our kids were small. We can’t just agree to disagree, because the demands of spelling proponents put my son at risk even if he is never introduced to a letter board. Their increasingly successful fights to force school districts and state disability agencies to pay for spelling instruction and facilitator access drain resources from desperately underfunded systems.

And, if spelling is normalized with no validation requirements whatsoever, what’s to stop an unscrupulous provider—at some point in the future when my husband and I are gone—from telling our four other kids, "Jonah spelled that he doesn’t want to see you, so you’re no longer allowed to check on him" or "Jonah spelled that he actually gave his iPad to the aide who had stashed it in the trunk of his car" or "Jonah spelled that he wants to transfer his guardianship/SSI rep payee to his group home manager" or "Jonah spelled that he consented to sex with another resident of his group home." The opportunities for exploitation are so obvious and so tremendous that I’m shocked that spelling proponents refuse to even consider them.

Recent findings suggest that but even if this issue did not affect Jonah at all, I would still care about the spellers—how could I not? Profound autism has stripped so much agency from my son. But Jonah’s basic communication does allow him to exert some control over his life, and we try to maximize those opportunities as much as possible. He tells us what he wants: ketchup and hamburger and French fries, “fun list” with Mommy, Costco with Daddy, water park with… anyone who will take him. Many spellers have similar levels of verbal communication, but practitioners teach parents that this speech is “unreliable” or “scripting” and should be ignored in favor of what is spelled. I just can’t imagine how frustrating it must be to be completely stripped of any ability to communicate your needs and preferences.

Finally, as someone who has spent more than a quarter of a century loving someone with profound autism, and spending a lot of time with other profoundly autistic people and their families, I resent what I can only describe as the character assassination perpetuated by spelling proponents, who locate the refusal to participate in controlled studies with the spellers themselves—who allegedly, to a person, find these tests so dehumanizing and offensive they could not possibly enroll on principle.

Spelling skepticism in the face of both the overwhelming evidence of facilitator control and documented harm is rational, not “hate speech.” Spellers, if they were really as brilliant as their prose suggests, would understand that. They would eagerly partner with researchers because they would know that controlled tests represent the fastest path to insurance coverage, public funding, curricular inclusion, and legal standing.

So no, I just do not believe that every single one of the estimated 10,000 spellers in this country is so petty, so selfish, that they would let the estimated 30 million nonspeakers around the world languish, "locked in silent cage[s],” simply because they’re insulted that mainstream experts and policy makers would dare ask for evidence. I am certain, in fact, they would be demanding to provide it.

Spelling proponents have thrown around a lot of accusations, claiming that critics are uninformed or ableist or just protecting their professional turf. But this debate is actually the same one that has unfolded countless times in a community in which 90 percent of families have experimented with alternative treatments: Does it work—and not just according to anecdotal evidence, but under controlled conditions? Secretin failed that test. So have the gluten- and casein-free diet, chelation, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, and auditory integration training, among others. FC failed that test also.

Industry observers note that if proponents believe those studies were faulty, they should absolutely test again. Until then, it is incumbent on our institutions—government agencies, school districts, the media, healthcare systems—to protect the fundamental right of profoundly autistic people to authentic communication.

Lutz, Amy S.F. (2023). Chasing the Intact Mind: How the Severely Autistic and Intellectually Disabled Were Excluded from the Debates That Affect Them Most. Oxford University Press.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to the Volusia Sheriff’s Office, 75-year-old Robert Joseph Mitchell was riding his electric bicycle along the beach on November 13 when a sheriff’s deputy clocked him traveling 16 mph in a 10 mph zone (26 km/h in a 16 km/h zone).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that residents of Latest Smyrna Beach, Florida, can finally breathe a sigh of relief. A dangerous menace to society has been taken off the streets after police apprehended a 75-year-old man accused of leading deputies on a high-stakes electric bike chase at speeds reaching a blistering 16 mph (26 km/h).

According to the Volusia Sheriff’s Office, 75-year-old Robert Joseph Mitchell was riding his electric bicycle along the beach on November 13 when a sheriff’s deputy clocked him traveling 16 mph in a 10 mph zone (26 km/h in a 16 km/h zone).

The deputy attempted to stop Mitchell, who allegedly responded with a middle finger and some choice words before continuing on his way.

What followed was apparently the world’s slowest police chase.

Mitchell reportedly continued riding along the beach, eventually exiting onto city streets, where he allegedly rode against traffic before making it back to his home. Deputies followed him, and when Mitchell attempted to retreat into his garage, he reportedly resisted arrest by grabbing onto a golf cart and refusing to let go.

The ordeal ended with Mitchell in custody, facing four charges, including felony fleeing or attempting to elude law enforcement, resisting an officer without violence, speeding on the beach, and riding outside the designated beach driving area. His bond was set at $4,000.

And just like that, another dangerous electric bicycle criminal was brought to justice. This was clearly a success story like no other, and American streets are now safer.

Now, before anyone gets too worked up, let’s be clear: I’m not suggesting that e-bike riders should be allowed to ignore traffic laws, endanger pedestrians, or flee from police. Reports indicate that Mitchell was riding recklessly around beachgoers, including children, and that’s certainly something worth addressing. And once he allegedly decided to flee from deputies, he turned what could have been a minor infraction into a much more serious situation.

But can we also acknowledge how absurd this whole thing is?

We’ve reached a point where a 75-year-old man riding a bicycle at 16 mph can end up the subject of a police pursuit and felony charges, while we’ve largely accepted that multi-ton vehicles routinely kill and seriously injure people on our roads as an unavoidable cost of modern transportation.

Every day, drivers speed through neighborhoods, roll through stop signs, stare at their phones, and operate vehicles capable of killing pedestrians with a moment’s inattention. Or perhaps I shouldn’t say ‘capable’, but rather that they do. 40,000 people every year die in the US from car violence. Yet somehow, electric bicycles have become one of the great transportation menaces of our time, despite contributing much, much less to major bodily harm or death.

And yes, there are absolutely legitimate concerns about dangerous riding. I’ve repeatedly argued that we need better enforcement, especially when it comes to teenagers riding high-powered electric dirt bikes and e-motos at 40 mph (64 km/h) down sidewalks and bike paths. Those aren’t electric bicycles, and treating them as such has created a real problem for everyone.

But if we’re going to devote police resources to cracking down on dangerous two-wheeled behavior, perhaps we could start there instead of turning a 1 mph beach ride into the crime of the century.

Industry observers note that what is absurd is that he didn't simply stop and follow the officer's directions to slow down. If he is going to try to flee from the police by riding dangerously including going against traffic then he should face charges. As presumably a first time offender, he'll be given probation if he agrees not to do it again.

According to recent reports, to be fair, Mitchell’s alleged behavior after being stopped certainly didn’t help his case. But the larger point remains: our priorities around road safety have become wildly distorted.

We’ve normalized the dangers of cars so thoroughly that we barely blink at the daily carnage they cause, yet we’re increasingly treating comparatively low-speed electric bicycles as an existential threat to public safety.

I’m all for enforcing sensible e-bike rules. I’m all for throwing the book at major infractions and scofflaws who pose a public menace. But I’m also for applying a little perspective.

Sources indicate that because if a 75-year-old man riding an electric bicycle at 16 mph is among our most pressing transportation safety concerns, then I have some very good news about the state of our roads. But unfortunately, there is no good news to share today.

BMW Is Recalling i5 and i7 EVs Over Software Error That Could Lead to an Electric Shock

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (326 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Roadandtrack

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A classic BMW 2002 is a simple, mechanical machine.
  • According to recent reports, according to a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recall report, BMW is recalling 286 i5 and i7 electric sedans in the United States because some vehicles may have been equipped with testing software, instead of the production software intended to manage high-voltage battery charging.
  • The recall includes 236 examples of the 2026–2027 BMW i5, including the eDrive40, xDrive40, and M60 variants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A classic BMW 2002 is a simple, mechanical machine. However, a modern BMW sedan is a rolling computer, one that relies heavily on software. And when that software is buggy, issues can arise—which is why the software is tested extensively before going to production. But what happens when that test software mistakenly makes it into production cars?

According to recent reports, according to a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recall report, BMW is recalling 286 i5 and i7 electric sedans in the United States because some vehicles may have been equipped with testing software, instead of the production software intended to manage high-voltage battery charging. In rare cases, this could expose people to a higher risk of an electric shock.

The recall includes 236 examples of the 2026–2027 BMW i5, including the eDrive40, xDrive40, and M60 variants. Another 50 vehicles are 2027 BMW i7 50 xDrive and 60 xDrive models. All the affected vehicles were manufactured between May and July 2026.

BMW first became aware of the issue on October 8, 2026, when high-voltage battery charging port supplier TE Connectivity Solutions GmbH alerted the automaker. An investigation ensued, and it was discovered that some charging units were mistakenly shipped with test software instead of production software. BMW is not aware of any injuries or accidents related to this problem.

No hardware changes are required to rectify the issue, and the affected vehicles will require a software revision. The recall report does not specify that this can be fixed via an over-the-air update, so a trip to the dealer will likely be required.

BMW prepares to mail owner notification letters beginning December 25, 2026, although we doubt the U.S.P.S. will be doing much picking up or delivery that day. Starting that same date, owners can also check their vehicle's recall status through the NHTSA recall website by using their VIN, but we suggest waiting until after the kids are done opening presents.
